item.title: Separating Field--Camp Alignment from Structural Balance in a Frustrated Random-Field Ising Model of Social Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.12578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frustrated Ising models of social networks mix ferromagnetic (agreement-seeking) and antiferromagnetic (antagonistic) couplings, and the antagonistic bonds are almost always placed independently at a fixed rate, yielding a +/-J spin glass. Real signed networks (Epinions, Slashdot, Wikipedia) instead show an excess of balanced triads, and perfectly balanced placement is gauge-equivalent to an unfrustrated ferromagnet. We compare three sign-placement conditions on a frustrated random-field Ising model of a polarised population, sharing an identical graph, field assignment, and edge-weight magnitudes: an independent baseline; a balance-structured condition whose camp membership coincides with each voter's field sign; and the same condition with camp labels randomly permuted, so triadic balance is identical by construction while the camp-field correlation is removed. On a confound-controlled Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of the sampled energy-gap distribution (simulated annealing), the aligned condition differs from the baseline at every density tested (p = 7.3e-8), while the permuted condition shows no significant difference (paired mean difference 0.003, 95% CI [-0.041, 0.046]). Field-camp alignment, not triadic balance alone, drives the effect. The qualitative direction follows from a known mapping; the contribution is a quantitative, confound-controlled measurement of the effect's size away from that limit, robust to parallel-tempering sampling, system sizes up to N = 300, and structural noise calibrated to real networks, while triadic balance alone produces no detectable effect at N = 90 and at most a small one at N = 180-300 (paired change in KS distance about 0.04, 95% CI upper bound below 0.09).
item.dc:creator: Natalia Romero

item.title: Credit Attribution in Timestamped Soccer Networks Using Multivariate Hawkes Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.12775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The two main traditional player statistics used in soccer are goals scored and assists, with an assist credited when a player's pass immediately leads to a teammate scoring. Attributing credit solely to the player who makes the final pass before a goal fails to account for the contributions of multiple players in the buildup to the goal. Consequently, traditional statistics provide only a limited view of player involvement. In this paper, we use multivariate Hawkes processes (MHPs) to model timestamped sequences of passes and shots, which form continuous-time networks. MHPs provide a branching mechanism where an event (a pass or shot) can be generated as a child of a previous event, which allows us to quantify each pass's contribution to a subsequent pass or shot. This approach distributes credit across multiple passes within an attacking sequence, making it applicable across a wide range of situations. Building on this framework, we propose expected goal involvements (xGI), a metric that measures a player's involvement in creating goal scoring opportunities based on their passes. This metric identifies players who play key roles in creating goal scoring opportunities even if they do not make the final pass, offering a more comprehensive measure of attacking involvement and player performance.
item.dc:creator: Phillip W. Kornberg, Kevin S. Xu

item.title: Les Mis\'erables Dialogue: A film-based network representation of social communication
item.description: arXiv:2610.13148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we revisit the classic Les Mis\'erables benchmark network from the perspective of social communication. Using the 1998 film adaptation of the novel, we construct the publicly available Les Mis\'erables Dialogue temporal text network, which explicitly distinguishes speakers, addressees, and other recipients of each utterance, along with its content and timing. Using the ten social dimensions model, we also derive multilayer network representations of the network, in which layers correspond to distinct relational dimensions. Beyond the network dataset, this work offers a general methodology for building similarly rich communication datasets from similar narrative sources.
item.dc:creator: Theodora Moldovan, Georgios Panayiotou, Davide Vega

item.title: Extracting Illicit-Rich Subgraph from Transaction Networks via Feed-Guided Shortest Paths
item.description: arXiv:2610.13280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study investigative subgraph extraction for Anti-Money Laundering (AML) transaction graphs using the Shortest Paths Network Search Algorithm (SPNSA), which aggregates shortest paths among a small input feed of entities. Since SPNSA is highly sensitive to the feed choice, we evaluate several graph-only feed selection strategies and propose a motif-based coherent feed selection method. Experiments on the IBM-AML benchmark (HI-Small, LI-Small, HI-Medium) and the Elliptic Bitcoin transaction graph show that the proposed strategy yields markedly higher illicit ratios in the extracted subgraph than random and degree-based heuristics on Elliptic and the IBM-AML HI variants, while keeping the output compact.
item.dc:creator: Doniyor Koshimbetov (Ko\c{c} University, Istanbul, T\"urkiye), E. \c{S}ule Yaz{\i}c{\i} (Ko\c{c} University, Istanbul, T\"urkiye), Asha Rao (RMIT University, Melbourne, Australia)

item.title: Polarization Dynamics under Algorithmic Recommendations in LLM-based Online Social Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.13351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How do recommendation algorithms contribute to the formation of polarized opinions in online social networks? This question has been studied through empirical analyses of real platforms and mathematical models of opinion dynamics. Empirical studies capture user behavior but are often limited by noisy, incomplete, or inaccessible platform data, while mathematical models offer control and interpretability but usually rely on simplified opinion update rules. More recently, large language model (LLM)-based social simulations have provided an alternative for studying recommendation and opinion dynamics through natural-language interactions. However, how different ways of applying recommendations shape opinion dynamics remains underexplored. In this work, we provide a controlled comparison of two different recommendation mechanisms in an LLM-based online social network simulation. Edge Recommendation (ER) introduces new connections in the network, while Content-Exposure Recommendation (CR) exposes additional users to individual posts without modifying the underlying graph. Our framework represents users as LLM-based agents who interact in natural language while maintaining evolving opinion states. We measure polarization as opinion dispersion, extremization as the average distance of opinions from the neutral midpoint, and reinforcement as interactions that amplify already aligned opinions. Our results show higher mean polarization and extremization across recommendation conditions compared with the no-recommendation baseline, with absolute differences of up to $0.12$ in our main experiments.
item.dc:creator: Ali Safarpoor Dehkordi, Mohammad Shirzadi, Mehwish Nasim, Ahad N. Zehmakan

item.title: A Multi-Dimensional Score for Detecting Lesser-Known Points of Interest in Mountain Regions
item.description: arXiv:2610.13467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Overtourism concentrates visitor demand on few iconic sites, while other points of interest (POIs) in the same area often remain known only to a narrower public. This imbalance is especially critical in mountain environments, where limited infrastructure amplifies environmental pressures. Discovering lesser-known POIs is relevant for redistributing tourism demand spatially, valuing underrepresented heritage, and temporally, easing high seasonality pressures on popular POIs. Across the literature, definitions of lesser-known POIs or hidden gems remain scattered, and existing scoring approaches remain incomplete, relying on narrow indicators (e.g., number of photos, reviews, likes) which fail to characterize mountain POIs holistically. These approaches are further constrained by their reliance on commercial proprietary sources, or by questionnaires that are subject to memory bias. To address these gaps, we introduce a novel multi-dimensional metric, the Obscurity Score, that groups fragmented literature into four key dimensions (International Awareness, Attractiveness, Promotion, and Accessibility) to systematically detect and characterize lesser-known POIs and enable their promotion as a first step toward mitigating overtourism. To operationalize this score, we develop a generic pipeline mapping open data sources onto these four dimensions. Preliminary results from a web-based prototype demonstrate the practical relevance of the proposed approach.

item.title: Teams without teams: a trace-based method for measuring team-like organization
item.description: arXiv:2610.13529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital platforms provide increasingly detailed traces of collaborative activity, yet these traces do not directly reveal whether contributions remain largely independent or whether more structured forms of collective work emerge through interaction. This paper addresses the methodological problem of measuring such organization when the collective being studied is not defined as a team in advance. We propose a trace-based method for measuring teamness, understood as the degree to which collaborative activity expresses properties associated with teamwork. The method translates established dimensions of teamwork into behavioral indicators that can be recovered from digital traces. These indicators can be examined separately and summarized through a composite measure of their joint expression. It does not require predefined team membership and is designed to be adapted across collaborative settings. We illustrate the method using revision histories from 52,437 articles in the English Wikipedia's Medicine WikiProject, comprising more than 10 million human-authored edits. Using article-months as observation units, the application shows that different dimensions of teamlike organization display distinct patterns and that their joint expression can vary within the same articles over time. The contribution is a general measurement framework for examining graded and dynamic forms of collective organization directly from behavioral traces.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Computational Social Science, 2026, 9 (4), pp.65

item.title: Non-Bayesian Social Learning with Heterogeneous and Time-Varying Aggregation Rules
item.description: arXiv:2610.13611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People constantly form opinions by combining what they observe with what friends, collegues, and communities tell them. Following this idea, this article generalizes earlier results in Non-Bayesian social learning on strongly connected social networks, where agents repeatedly update their beliefs by combining their own private signals with the beliefs of their neighbors. Previous work assumed that every agent aggregates information in the same way and often does not change in time, assuming agents never change how they reason and listen to others. We show that agents' beliefs still converge almost surely to the true state when agents use heterogeneous and time-varying (non-stochastic) aggregation rules under certain conditions. That is, even when people change their way to aggregate others opinions, the community can still reach the truth as long as information flows among its members. We also provide convergence rate results under this scenario and show that, for some of these functions, it is at least equal to the best convergence rate we have found in the literature. We present the widely used aggregation functions in the Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) family as a specific case of our general model, which include rules such as the log-linear, DeGroot, and the harmonic rules, and provide a simple illustrative example to show the capabilities of the model.
item.dc:creator: Sammy Oukaci, Pol Rodr\'iguez Farr\'es, Jesus Cerquides

item.title: How Social Reinforcement Shapes Word-of-Mouth: A Conviction-Based Model for Marketing Diffusion and Network Targeting
item.description: arXiv:2610.13890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organizations increasingly rely on social networks to drive product adoption and word-of-mouth diffusion, yet a central challenge is that consumers differ not only in whether they adopt but also in how strongly they subsequently advocate. In particular, individuals who adopt under strong social reinforcement often develop greater conviction and become more persuasive. Existing diffusion models largely abstract away from this mechanism by treating influence strength as static. We introduce a conviction-based diffusion framework, the Pressure Threshold (PT) model, that captures how social reinforcement shapes both adoption and subsequent advocacy. In this model, an individual's influence increases with the cumulative social pressure experienced at adoption, providing a tractable representation of conviction formation while preserving the interpretability of classical threshold-based models. We study the managerial implications of this mechanism through marketing targeting and seeding. We show that accounting for reinforcement fundamentally alters optimal targeting strategies, shifting emphasis toward consumers in cohesive network regions where repeated exposure can amplify downstream word-of-mouth. While reinforcement introduces nonstandard features into the optimization problem, we demonstrate that scalable heuristics remain effective and provide data-dependent performance guarantees. Across synthetic and real-world networks, we find that reinforcement often substantially increases the effectiveness of seeding interventions, particularly in dense and clustered environments where opportunities for social validation are abundant. Using time-stamped social media cascades, we further show that the PT model improves predictive accuracy relative to standard diffusion models, highlighting the empirical relevance of conviction-driven amplification.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek K. Umrawal, Curt Stutsman, Camille Woods, Eliot W. Robson

item.title: Learning Social Influence with Unobserved Attention
item.description: arXiv:2610.12616v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Social influence, the tendency of our social environment to sway our beliefs and behaviors, is often cited as a driver of population-level trends in opinions or beliefs. Many quantitative theories of social influence assume that an agent interacts with its entire social environment. This assumption is often unrealistic. For example, users of online platforms typically see posts from only a small subset of the accounts they follow at any given time. We introduce a simple probabilistic agent-based model of social influence that explicitly models unobserved attention mechanisms. The first of these latent mechanisms is selection: each agent interacts with only one other agent at a time from its social environment. The second is retention: the agent chooses whether or not to ignore the opinion of the other. Our model admits an efficient maximum-likelihood algorithm which allows us to fit it to opinion traces even when these mechanisms are unobserved. On synthetic data, omitting either latent mechanism reduces the overall strength of social influence governed by the inferred interaction kernel, which hides the evidence for the underlying nonlinearity of the social influence. We study a selection of previously analyzed empirical datasets and curate several new ones. We show that models that include the latent mechanisms are often more predictive on these datasets; indeed, they typically improve prediction far more than the choice of interaction kernel does. Modeling latent attention increases held-out predictive likelihood on 14 of these 15 datasets. Each mechanism changes the size of the inferred kernel in a predictable direction, while its effect on the kernel's shape depends on the data.
item.dc:creator: William Thompson, Moyi Tian, Linh Huynh, Alexander Wiedemann, Vicki Modisette, Philip S. Chodrow, Heather Z. Brooks

item.title: Onions in the ATmosphere: Decentralizing Trust in Identity
item.description: arXiv:2610.12764v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiple approaches have been implemented for identities that associate meaningful identifiers, such as domain names, with self-authenticating identifiers, such as onion addresses. While these approaches offer various advantages both from identifier meaningfulness and from identifier self-authentication, identifier association itself is subject to blocking, hijack, fingerprinting, and other forms of surveillance and manipulation. So too are the resources associated with an identity comprising a meaningful identifier and a self-authenticating identifier. This paper describes ongoing work on two such approaches to self-authenticating meaningful identity (SAMI): associating a registered domain name with an onion address (onion association) and associating an atproto handle with a decentralized identifier (DID association). We present both the application of already implemented and published means of secure onion association to DID association and the combination of both in a single identity. Finally, we describe grounding identity association and integrity in contextual trust, wherein trusting attestations of identity relies on contextual relevance of an attestor to the identity rather than relying only on structural authority, for example as embodied in the traditional centralized infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Paul Syverson, Nick Gerakines

item.title: BenCoDiC: A Large-Scale Contextual Cyberbullying Corpus for Bengali Political News Discourse FULL VERSION
item.description: arXiv:2610.13121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cyberbullying is a growing concern in online communities, yet existing Bengali corpora remain limited in contextual information, annotation transparency, scale, accessibility, and support for multidimensional analysis, thereby hindering robust detection and comprehensive study of harasser behaviors and networks. To address these gaps, we introduce the Bengali Contextual and Diverse Cyberbullying (\textit{BenCoDiC}) corpus, a publicly available contextual cyberbullying resource for Bengali political news discourse comprising 50,250 textual instances collected from 100 YouTube videos and their associated discussions. The corpus preserves caption--comment--reply relationships and is organized through a nine-dimensional star schema covering users, videos, textual content, context, time, engagement, political parties, target identities, and language categories. Five AI chatbots were initially evaluated for annotation but did not meet the predefined reliability criterion. Consequently, a two-tier human annotation process with expert verification was adopted, achieving Fleiss' $\kappa=0.86$ and Krippendorff's $\alpha=0.86$. Statistical analyses characterize the corpus, while transformer-based experiments show that incorporating conversational context yields modest but consistent improvements over isolated-text classification. \textit{BenCoDiC} supports context-aware cyberbullying detection and perpetrator-oriented behavioral and network analysis. The corpus is available at https://github.com/bencodic/BenCoDiC-Corpus.
item.dc:creator: Md. Nesarul Hoque, Rudra Pratap Deb Nath, Umme Salma, Shima Chakraborty, Md. Hanif Seddiqui

item.title: Predicting Social Media Engagement using Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.16082v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Social media platforms are popular channels for disseminating information, owing to their large user bases and ease of access. Companies also use social media as an important aspect of the advertising process. By creating high-quality posts, companies can strengthen their engagement metrics and increase their follower count. While a growing body of research has examined social media engagement, fewer studies have jointly examined the visual, textual, and temporal features of image posts, even though these features collectively determine the performance of content on social media. To understand the important drivers of social media engagement, we collect image posts of furniture firms on Facebook and extract visual, temporal, and textual features from them using text and image analytics methods. We evaluate several machine learning models--including Random Forest, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)--to assess the drivers and the prediction power of social media engagement using the features from our data. Our primary model, LightGBM, explains 81.8% of the variance in the engagement score, 2.3 times that of our baseline model. We observed that brand-relative deviation features, which capture how far a post departs from its brand's norms, are the strongest predictors, accounting for 51.3% of total importance. Our research quantifies the extent to which these features are associated with interactions and provides recommendations that organizations may consider.
item.dc:creator: Ritwik Singh, Mayukh Majumdar, Subodha Kumar
